title: How Often Does Leptospirosis Have a Biphasic Presentation in Tropical Australia?
content: Objectives: Leptospirosis is classically described as having a biphasic presentation: an initial “leptospiraemic phase” characterised by fever, headache and myalgia followed by an “immune phase”, coinciding with the appearance of IgM antibodies during the second week of illness, when more severe, end-organ manifestations are said to develop. We performed this study to determine how frequently patients with leptospirosis truly present in this manner in tropical Australia. Methods: We examined consecutive cases of laboratory-confirmed leptospirosis admitted to an Australian referral hospital between January 2015 and June 2024 and correlated the patients’ clinical course with their laboratory findings. A patient was said to have a biphasic presentation if they reported a >24-hour period of defervescence or diminution in symptoms prior to presentation or during their hospitalisation. We also recorded 90-day mortality and documented hospital re-presentations within 90 days with immune-mediated complications of leptospirosis. Results: The median (interquartile range, IQR) duration of symptoms in the 111 patients was 3 (2-4) days; only 2 reported >9 days of symptoms and no patient reported a >24-hour diminution in symptoms prior to their presentation. In total, 56/111 (50%) were admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) after a median (IQR) of 4 (3-5) days of symptoms. Of those who had diagnostic testing for leptospirosis performed on the day of their ICU admission, only 10/24 (42%) had a reactive IgM; all 25 who had polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of blood had a positive result. Recurrent, short-lived fever occurred in 7 patients during their hospitalisation: 6 were already intubated in ICU, the other was a child who did not receive antibiotics. There were no deaths or re-presentations to hospital with immune-mediated complications of leptospirosis within 90 days. Conclusions: A biphasic presentation of leptospirosis appears to be very rare in this region of tropical Australia.
